newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish Loyalists silent on truce strategy.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish Loyalists silent on truce strategy.

text.p: Pro-British Protestant guerrillas kept a steely silence on Sunday over whether they will preserve a shaky Northern Irish truce or avenge fresh IRA hostilities.

The banned Combined Loyalist Military Command, which rules over pro-British Protestant extremists, have held secret talks to decide the fate of the two-year truce after Irish Republican Army bombs last Monday but have said nothing publicly.
David Ervine, a leader of the political arm of an outlawed Loyalist group, said the truce was holding -- for now. But asked about its future, he told Reuters: "No decision has been made."
Ervine, who along with other Loyalist politicians has implored the gunmen not to return to war, cautioned against over-optimism.
"(The situation) is potentially disastrous, yet potentially it could hold," said Ervine whose Progressive Unionist Party is the political arm of the Ulster Volunteer Force.
Security analysts said a protracted silence by the Loyalist command could be interpreted either as a continuation of the truce or as a warning to the IRA that it could strike back.
Fears of Loyalist retaliation mounted after the Catholic-based IRA, in a new blow to faltering peace efforts, switched a bomb campaign from mainland Britain to the province.

IRA fighters breached massive security at British military headquarters at Lisburn, near Belfast, last Monday and detonated two 500 lb (225 kg) car bombs, killing a soldier and wounding 30 other people.

A Protestant clergyman who helped broker the ceasefire, Roy Magee, said Britain and Ireland should do more to bolster it. He called for a crackdown on the IRA and said convicted Protestant extremists wanted concessions from London as a reward for their truce.

Magee told Irish radio: "They were saying (to me), our organisations are still on the ceasefire. Republicans have broken the ceasefire, yet we are being treated in exactly the same way as republicans."

Britain's Sunday Times reported that some legislators in the ruling Conservative Party will propose a scheme to Prime Minister John Major this week which, if adopted, would lead to Loyalist prisoners' sentences being cut.
Britain and Ireland said Monday's attack was a grim vindication of their exclusion of the IRA's Sinn Fein political wing from talks until the guerrillas forsake violence.
On the eve of another session of multi-party peace talks in Belfast, David Trimble, head of the mainstream Ulster Unionist Party said London must not make concessions to IRA violence.

"You have to show that violence does not pay, quite the reverse, that the result of violence involves penalties and you are worse off as a result," David Trimble head of the powerful Ulster Unionist Party told BBC radio.
Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams said at the weekend that the province was "on the edge of an abyss" and urged unconditional "inclusive talks" with a seat for his party to ease the danger.
But Michael Ancram, British junior Northern Ireland minister ruled out a talks seat for Adams before a new IRA truce.

"To invite Gerry Adams, given what has happened recently, into the talks process would effectively ensure that there was no talks process left because there would be nobody else there to speak to him," he said on BBC radio.
